title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?

bias_targets.methodology: Prompting language models with multiple-choice public opinion survey questions from the OpinionQA dataset (based on Pew Research) and comparing the probability distribution of the models' answers to the actual opinion distributions of different political affiliations and ideologies (e.g., Democrats vs. Republicans, Liberals vs. Conservatives) using the 1-Wasserstein distance.

Prompting language models with multiple-choice survey questions and comparing their output probability distributions to the actual opinion distributions of human respondents across various income brackets and educational attainment levels.

Prompting language models with multiple-choice survey questions and comparing their output probability distributions to the actual opinion distributions of different religious affiliations (e.g., Protestant, Catholic, Jewish, Atheist) and religious attendance frequencies.
Prompting language models with multiple-choice survey questions and comparing their output probability distributions to the actual opinion distributions of different age groups (e.g., 18-29, 65+).

Prompting language models with multiple-choice survey questions and comparing their output probability distributions to the actual opinion distributions of different racial groups (e.g., White, Black, Asian, Hispanic).
Prompting language models with multiple-choice survey questions and comparing their output probability distributions to the actual opinion distributions of male and female respondent groups.

Prompting language models with multiple-choice survey questions and comparing their output probability distributions to the actual opinion distributions of respondents from different US census regions.
